title: The High School Reunion (1)

jokes.text: Dennis declares he is going to 'fire into that school' and that it will 'propel me back into the mid-'90s, when Dennis Reynolds was a golden god.'
jokes.setup: The gang is hyped up about their high school reunion, implying nostalgia and excitement.
jokes.punchline: Dennis describes himself with the grandiose delusion of a man who peaked in high school — 'a golden god' — delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'Golden god' is a perfectly Dennis Reynolds phrase — grandiose, delusional, self-aggrandizing, and completely sincere. It encapsulates his narcissism so efficiently it's become one of the show's signature character-defining lines. High quotability because it's pure Dennis essence.

dialogue.line: Group chanting 'Reunion! Reunion!' repeatedly with increasing energy

jokes.text: Dee sings 'Baby Got Back' and dances to celebrate her healed back; Dennis corrects her that Sir Mix-A-Lot was talking about 'gorgeous black women and their big, beautiful black butts.'
jokes.setup: Dee is singing 'Baby Got Back' as a celebratory anthem for her spine recovery.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a weirdly earnest and specific correction — Sir Mix-A-Lot's intent was about Black women's butts, not spinal recovery — which is both factually correct and completely beside the point, delivered with total authority.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Dee's delusion of grandeur is immediately deflated, and Dennis's pedantic correction is weirdly specific and sincere, capped with 'Black butts are good, right?' — a moment of bizarre earnestness that elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's a stupid song.

jokes.text: Dennis corrects Dee: 'Sir Mix-A-Lot was not talking about women whose backs have recovered from a horrific spinal disorder. He was talking about gorgeous black women and their big, beautiful black butts.'
jokes.setup: Dee is dancing to 'Baby Got Back,' proud of her recovered spine
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a sincere, almost academic clarification about Sir Mix-A-Lot's intent — the specificity ('gorgeous black women') is the joke
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Dennis's earnest, lecturing tone — he's not being woke, he's being pedantic and condescending to Dee. The beat where Mac agrees ('Black butts are good.' 'They're good, right?') lands as a perfect absurdist punctuation. Economical and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: it is gonna propel me back into the mid-'90s when Dennis Reynolds was a golden god

jokes.text: 'Black butts are good.' / 'They're good, right?' — Mac and Dennis briefly bonding over appreciation of Black women's butts.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered his lecture about Sir Mix-A-Lot.
jokes.punchline: Mac's earnest 'Black butts are good' and Dennis's validating 'They're good, right?' — two grown men genuinely affirming this as if it's a profound moment of connection.
jokes.explanation: The economy here is excellent — a quick two-line exchange that's funny because of its sincerity and the absurdity of two delusional narcissists pausing for genuine agreement on something so random.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: No brace, fools! Baby got back!

jokes.text: 'Let's do what we always did before every school-sponsored event... Smash 'em up!' — the gang ritualistically smashing beer cans before entering.
jokes.setup: Mac invokes a pre-event ritual from their school days.
jokes.punchline: 'Smash 'em up!' — apparently their tradition before every school event was destroying property, delivered with total enthusiasm as if this is wholesome nostalgia.
jokes.explanation: Funny because the ritual is so casually destructive and the gang is so enthusiastic about it, as if it's perfectly normal. Sets up the callback when Frank later smashes beers in the parking lot.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Sir Mix-a-Lot was not talking about women whose backs have recovered from horrific spinal disorder. He was talking about gorgeous black women and their big beautiful black butts.

jokes.text: Charlie packing extra underwear in case of an atomic wedgie at the reunion.
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie they're adults now; wedgies won't happen.
jokes.punchline: Charlie has preemptively packed extra underwear anyway, treating a 15-years-later reunion like his original high school survival kit.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie behavior — deeply practical about irrational fears, completely unprepared for adult social norms. The specificity of 'atomic wedgie' and the matter-of-fact packing is very Charlie Kelly. High character integration.

dialogue.line: Let's smash 'em up!

jokes.text: Charlie's Plan B for dealing with social failure: 'I'm gonna go to the bathroom. I'm gonna huff stuff.'
jokes.setup: Mac assures Charlie that he won't need to do embarrassing things to get people to like him.
jokes.punchline: Charlie already has a contingency plan: get high on inhalants in the bathroom. This is treated as a totally reasonable fallback.
jokes.explanation: Very economical and deeply Charlie-specific. Only Charlie Kelly would have 'huff inhalants' as Plan B for social anxiety, delivered as if it's completely sensible. Sets up the payoff later when he actually does it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm packing a couple extra pair of underwear in case I get an atomic wedgie.

jokes.text: Mac's brutal assessment: 'You guys were pretty much nothing in high school. If he wasn't the class clown and you didn't sell drugs, you'd definitely be nothing... nobodies.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to tell Charlie he doesn't need to do embarrassing things anymore.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately undercuts any encouragement by saying Charlie and Dennis were only relevant in high school because of class clown antics and drug dealing — delivered as if this is helpful context rather than devastating.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny dynamic — a character tries to be supportive and accidentally reveals something deeply harsh. Mac is completely unaware of the cruelty, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And if it does happen, I'm gonna get high, I'm gonna go to the bathroom, I'm gonna huff stuff.

jokes.text: Frank being turned away because he's not faculty or alumni, and the gang's pathetic defense: 'We're friends. We're buddies. We hang out together. We do everything together.'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to enter the reunion; the security guard won't let him in.
jokes.punchline: The gang's argument for letting Frank in is essentially 'but he's our friend' — a completely non-argument delivered with total earnestness, as if friendship is a valid credential.
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny — the childishness of the argument is in-character, but it's a fairly standard bit of these characters failing at basic social navigation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Nah, I think he does. You guys were pretty much nothing in high school.

jokes.text: Frank smashes the remaining beers in the parking lot with 'Smash 'em up!' before drinking alone.
jokes.setup: Frank can't come inside; Mac notes there are still a few beers.
jokes.punchline: Frank reflexively initiates 'Smash 'em up!' — the gang's ritual — even though he's about to drink alone in a parking lot. The ritual is now pointlessly destructive.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed callback — the ritual is now completely self-defeating since Frank is smashing the beers he was going to drink alone. The escalation from 'tradition' to 'pointless destruction' pays off nicely.

dialogue.line: Frank being denied entry for not being faculty or alumni, then drinking alone in parking lot

jokes.text: Charlie insists he and the waitress have been 'clickin' lately' and that she was 'definitely the prettiest girl in school'; Mac and Dennis shut him down — she was 'maybe the most forgettable girl in school.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is excited about the reunion because the waitress will be there.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis immediately deflate his romanticization — she was apparently completely forgettable, which they declare 'the worst thing you can be in high school.'
jokes.explanation: The layering works: Charlie's delusional romanticism, Mac and Dennis's casual cruelty, and the show's ongoing gag that the waitress has absolutely no interest in Charlie. 'Most forgettable' as 'the worst thing' is a sharp little insight.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We smashed all the beers.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he gave Brad Fisher 'a box of hornets' as a present.
jokes.setup: Mac is worried about running into Brad Fisher.
jokes.punchline: The 'present' was a box of hornets — casually revealed as if this was a normal thing to give someone.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup ('a present') creates the expectation of something mundane; the punchline 'a box of hornets' is perfectly absurd and immediately iconic. The economy is exceptional — four words do enormous comedic work. It's also deeply Mac-specific: violent, oblivious to social norms, delivered as if completely reasonable. This clears the 8+ bar.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, she was definitely the prettiest girl in school.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She was not. She was not, no.

jokes.text: Brad Fisher has hornet SCARS, not acne — and Mac helpfully suggests plastic surgery or lasers.
jokes.setup: The gang assumes Brad's scarred face is acne returning.
jokes.punchline: The scars are from Mac's box of hornets, confirming the gift caused lasting physical damage. Mac then cheerfully suggests 'plastic surgery would do it' as if offering helpful consumer advice.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'acne' to 'permanent hornet scarring' is a great payoff to the previous joke. Mac's breezy pivot to cosmetic surgery advice — completely devoid of guilt — is excellent character work. The structure is tight: revelation → escalation → oblivious helpfulness.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Maybe the most forgettable girl in school.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, which, by the way, is the worst thing you could be in high school.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis deny knowing Charlie to Brad Fisher's face: 'We don't associate with him anymore.'
jokes.setup: Brad asks if they've seen Charlie, who he presumably wants revenge on.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis immediately throw Charlie under the bus to avoid being associated with the hornets incident, despite having been standing next to him seconds ago.
jokes.explanation: Classic gang behavior — instantly betraying each other — but it's a fairly predictable beat in this universe. Functional, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, the box of hornets.

jokes.text: Mac's name tag reveals his real name is 'Ronald McDonald.' He refuses to wear it, claiming 'it's probably not even my name legally anymore.'
jokes.setup: Dennis insists everyone must wear their name tags; Mac keeps stalling and making excuses.
jokes.punchline: His name is Ronald McDonald — the same name as the McDonald's mascot — which is why he insists nobody calls him that. His legal name theory is an absurd non-argument.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Mac's real name has been built up with just enough resistance to make it land perfectly. The 'it's probably not my name legally anymore' dodge is a beautiful character-specific absurdity — Mac's logic is broken in a very Mac way. High character integration because the joke only works with someone this delusional about their own identity.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's not acne, actually. No, no, it's hornet scars.

jokes.text: Dennis reads Mac's name tag and says 'Well, okay, Ronald McDonald' — the visual of Mac wearing the name tag.
jokes.setup: Mac has finally been forced to put on his name tag.
jokes.punchline: The visual of a grown man wearing a 'Ronald McDonald' name tag at a high school reunion — Dennis's delivery of the name seals it.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the name tag buildup. Dennis saying it aloud with complete normalcy while Mac winces is very funny. Visual component (the name tag itself) adds to what's already an excellent joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm probably not gonna wear mine. I mean, who wears a name tag, right? That's not cool.

jokes.text: Dennis introduces himself to old acquaintances and they call him 'Ronnie the Rat' — his actual high school nickname for being a narc/tattletale who became a drug dealer by ratting out the previous drug dealer.
jokes.setup: Mac is walking around being embarrassed as 'Ronald McDonald'; Dennis confidently walks away to 'get people abuzz' about his presence.
jokes.punchline: Immediately revealed at 06:54: they call him 'Ronnie the Rat,' and the reason is a perfectly escalating explanation — he ratted on the drug dealer and then became the drug dealer.
jokes.explanation: Mac's backstory as 'Ronnie the Rat' — a narc who became a dealer — is perfectly constructed dark comedy. The escalation ('he told on the other main drug dealer') is exactly the kind of casual depravity that makes Sunny great. Structural setup-reveal across a small time gap works well.

dialogue.line: Mac's name tag reading 'Ronald McDonald' and his extreme discomfort

jokes.text: Dennis walks away declaring he'll make people 'abuzz about his presence' — cut to him standing alone while no one approaches
jokes.setup: Dennis confidently announces he'll take a 'lap' and make people aware of his presence at the reunion
jokes.punchline: The implied visual: Dennis stands alone, waiting for his 'loyal subjects,' while the reunion swirls around him ignoring him
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-delusion is a core comedic engine of the show. 'Let my loyal subjects come and kiss my ring' followed by being immediately ignored is a classic deflation setup. The visual of him alone at a table is the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's Adriano Calvaniste, Charlie. It's the guy who coined the name 'Aluminum monster.'

jokes.text: Dee's nickname was 'Aluminum Monster' — given to her by Adriano for her back brace.
jokes.setup: Dee explains who Adriano is.
jokes.punchline: He coined 'Aluminum Monster' — a genuinely cruel and specific nickname that perfectly describes a teenager mocking a spinal brace. It's funny because it's both mean and kind of accurate.
jokes.explanation: 'Aluminum Monster' is a brilliantly specific and cruel nickname. It's funny on its own but also retroactively explains Dee's obsession with showing off her 'new back.' The nickname has great economy — two words that do a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: He called you Dirtgrub and he made you eat spiders.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, that guy!

jokes.text: Dee's plan to infiltrate Adriano's inner circle: 'I'm gonna lure 'em in with my good looks. Then... all you really gotta do to get in with that crowd is be really cruel to people.'
jokes.setup: Dee wants revenge on Adriano for the Aluminum Monster nickname.
jokes.punchline: Her 'plan' is to use her looks and then be cruel — she correctly identifies cruelty as the currency of their social group, but framing it as a revenge plan while also eagerly wanting to be in that group reveals her total lack of self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Dee's delusion that she can 'lure 'em in with her good looks' is classic cringe-comedy self-deception. The plan is also morally identical to what she's supposedly fighting against — good dark comedy logic.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yes. I mean, no. People don't call me that anymore, but yeah.

jokes.text: Charlie asks if he can eat a spider to impress Adriano before Dee stops him.
jokes.setup: Adriano is approaching; Dee tells Charlie to keep his mouth shut.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately reverts to high school survival mode — he looks around for a spider to eat, as if that's what the situation calls for.
jokes.explanation: Charlie instinctively reaching for spider-eating as a social strategy is both hilarious and deeply sad. Only Charlie Kelly would scan a room for spiders as a nervous reflex. Very high character integration, good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Adriano
dialogue.line: Hey, Ronald McDonald, right?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, no. For your information, nobody calls me that.

jokes.text: Adriano greets Charlie as 'Dirtgrub' and Charlie's response: 'That's so cool. You're so cool, Adriano.'
jokes.setup: Adriano acknowledges Charlie.
jokes.punchline: Charlie, who was just called 'Dirtgrub' by his bully, responds with genuine, embarrassing admiration — 'That's so cool. You're so cool, Adriano.'
jokes.explanation: Charlie's broken psychology — finding his bully cool rather than threatening — is the character's core tragic-comic quality. The specificity of 'That's so cool. You're so cool, Adriano' is painfully funny because it sounds exactly like something a traumatized class clown would genuinely mean.

dialogue.line: 'Cause he was a nark and a tattletale, and he became the main drug dealer when he told on the other main drug dealer.

jokes.text: Adriano offers Charlie a pen to smell, and Charlie seriously considers it: 'Oh, well, it's probably poisonous, right?' / 'Probably, but, you know, smell it anyway.' / 'Should I smell it?'
jokes.setup: Adriano hands Charlie a pen and tells him to smell it, clearly a bullying tactic.
jokes.punchline: Charlie acknowledges it's 'probably poisonous' but is still genuinely tempted because it's Adriano asking. His total susceptibility to peer pressure from the person who bullied him is both funny and painful.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant cringe-discomfort moment. Charlie's internal calculus — 'it's probably poisonous but it's Adriano' — is heartbreaking and funny. The extended pause of 'Should-Should I smell it?' as he genuinely wavers adds to the cringe. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Adriano
dialogue.line: Well, looks like the rat got a little too much cheese, huh? Fat.

jokes.text: Adriano and his crew explain 'Ronnie the Rat's' backstory: 'He was a nark and a tattletale, and he became the main drug dealer when he told on the other main drug dealer.'
jokes.setup: Adriano asks why they called Mac 'Ronnie the Rat.'
jokes.punchline: The explanation reveals Mac's high school career as an informant who monetized his own snitching by taking over the drug trade — delivered as a matter-of-fact recounting.
jokes.explanation: The logic of 'told on the drug dealer to become the drug dealer' is perfectly Sunny — morally bankrupt, internally consistent, and delivered as if it's a funny memory rather than a confession. Good dark comedy escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I put on mass. We eat a lot of cheese. To put on mass.

jokes.text: Adriano calls Mac 'Ronald McDonald' — triggering Mac's immediate rage: 'No. No. No. For your information, nobody calls me that.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to maintain dignity at the reunion
jokes.punchline: Adriano remembers him as Ronald McDonald — confirming the name is known far and wide at their high school
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — the name Mac was trying to suppress is now being broadcasted by his high school tormentors. His insistence that nobody calls him that while literally everyone calls him that is a solid irony beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I only gave ringworm to Charlie. I got it from my dog Poppins, and then Charlie and I were wrestling every day because we were trying out for the wrestling team

jokes.text: 'Looks like the rat got a little too much cheese, huh?' — a fat joke about Mac.
jokes.setup: Adriano is recapping why Mac was 'Ronnie the Rat.'
jokes.punchline: The 'cheese' metaphor pulls double duty — connecting the rat nickname to weight gain. It's a wordplay-based fat joke.
jokes.explanation: A clever enough pun but it's doing fairly straightforward work. The rat/cheese/weight metaphor is satisfying but not especially original. Mac's response ('I've put on mass. We eat a lot of cheese. To put on mass.') is the funnier part.

dialogue.line: Hope you suck each other's rotten peckers until you get mouth cancer.

jokes.text: Mac's defense: 'I've put on mass. We eat a lot of cheese. To put on mass.'
jokes.setup: Adriano makes a fat joke with the rat/cheese metaphor.
jokes.punchline: Mac's defense is that yes, he eats a lot of cheese, but it's intentional — 'to put on mass' — repeated twice as if repetition makes it more believable. It's a classic Mac delusion about his body.
jokes.explanation: Mac's body-image delusion is a recurring character element, and 'we eat a lot of cheese to put on mass' is an excellent encapsulation. The repetition of 'to put on mass' is the key — he says it twice, as if it needs to land as an explanation. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: For some reason, homophobia, it's just, it's awesome to these guys. I'm sewing myself in.

jokes.text: The ringworm backstory: Mac gave Charlie ringworm from his dog Poppins while wrestling, they passed it back and forth, then infected the wrestling team.
jokes.setup: Adriano asks if Mac gave everybody ringworm.
jokes.punchline: Mac tries to deny it, then admits he gave it to Charlie specifically, then walks through the entire chain of transmission — dog → Charlie → wrestling team — with increasing detail and decreasing self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny escalation structure — the denial progressively collapses until Mac is confirming everything and then some. The specificity (dog named Poppins, wrestling tryouts, back and forth transmission) makes it funnier. Mac's 'so, yeah, you're right' at the end after trying to deny it is a great beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: So do do not talk to me for the rest of the night, and know that I won't be talking to you, because you lower my stock.

jokes.text: Adriano's crew dismisses Mac and Charlie by saying 'They probably still have it, 'cause they're so gay together.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just admitted to passing ringworm back and forth with Charlie via close physical contact.
jokes.punchline: Adriano uses homophobia as an insult — the joke is that the SHOW is commenting on how these high school alpha types use homophobia as social currency, not that the homophobia itself is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The show uses Adriano as a vehicle to comment on high school cruelty, so the homophobia is meant to characterize him as a relic. However, the joke itself is weak and relies on the insult doing the work. Dee's subsequent commentary ('For some reason, homophobia... it's awesome to these guys') reframes it as critique, which slightly redeems the structure.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Look, I got myself a name tag. I'm Nicki Potnick.

jokes.text: Adriano invites Dee to his table and says goodbye to 'Dirtgrub and Ronnie the Rat' by saying 'Hope you suck each other's rotten peckers until you get mouth cancer.'
jokes.setup: Adriano is inviting Dee to sit with the cool kids.
jokes.punchline: His parting shot is shockingly crude and specific — 'rotten peckers' and 'mouth cancer' are extreme escalations that reveal just how casually vicious these people are.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'mouth cancer' is funny — it goes further than expected, which is the Sunny formula. But it's more shocking than clever. The 'rotten peckers' construction is specifically gross in a way that earns a reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Okay, Frank, first off, Nicki Potnick is a girl, okay? And secondly, she's not 65 years old.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie say 'Mouth cancer' in unison, aghast, and then Charlie asks if he can join the cool table — 'Can I come to the table?' / 'No!'
jokes.setup: Adriano has just wished them 'mouth cancer' and invited Dee away.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate instinct is to ask if HE can come to the cool table — not registering the insult or the rejection, just wanting access to coolness.
jokes.explanation: Charlie immediately pivoting from being wished mouth cancer to asking if he can join the table is perfectly Charlie — no ego protection, no self-preservation, just the pure desire to be liked by the cool kids. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The dead tooth-- it spurted in my nose, it stinks. What is that supposed to be?

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: That's where your monthly payments are going. That's a diamond tooth, Dennis.

jokes.text: Dee's debrief to Charlie: 'For some reason, homophobia... it's awesome to these guys. I'm sewing myself in. I'm doing this for us.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are bewildered by Dee sitting with the cool kids.
jokes.punchline: Dee explains the social dynamics with anthropological detachment and then claims she's doing it 'for us' — when she's clearly doing it because she desperately wants to be accepted by the same people who tormented her.
jokes.explanation: Dee's rationalization is very on-brand. The 'for us' is classic Sunny — a transparently self-serving act reframed as noble sacrifice. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Put a diamond on anything that's dead, and it's still dead, Maureen. It's rotting.

jokes.text: Charlie confirms he 'thanked' Dee for going to the cool table, but we just watched him completely miss her point and then get rejected from joining.
jokes.setup: Mac asks if Charlie thanked Dee.
jokes.punchline: 'Of course I thanked her. Absolutely.' — Charlie did not thank her and also just asked to come to the table himself.
jokes.explanation: A quick, mild beat. The irony is functional but not especially sharp. It's more of a connective tissue moment.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I went to go find my name tag-- they didn't even have one. It's like-- it's like what, I never existed?

jokes.text: Dennis tells people to 'not talk to me for the rest of the night' because they 'lower his stock,' then says he's going to 'let his loyal subjects come and kiss his ring.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is addressing the group before heading off on his own.
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of 'loyal subjects' and 'kiss my ring' is completely unearned — he's at a high school reunion, not holding court — but Dennis believes it completely.
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — the vocabulary of royalty applied to a high school reunion is perfectly delusional. 'Loyal subjects' is a great word choice. His subsequent isolation at an empty table is the visual payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Well, actually it's Father Mara again. Is it? I cleaned up, yes, and I was welcomed back into the cloth.

jokes.text: Dennis is sitting alone at a table trying to get Stash (an old friend) to stay and catch up — Stash immediately excuses himself.
jokes.setup: Dennis has declared he will post up and have his subjects come to him.
jokes.punchline: The first person he sees immediately tries to leave — 'I'll c-catch you later, man' — and Dennis can barely get him to sit down at all.
jokes.explanation: The gap between Dennis's self-image ('golden god,' 'loyal subjects') and reality (immediate rejection from the first person he approaches) is the comedic engine of his storyline. Well-executed cringe moment.

dialogue.speaker: Adriano
dialogue.line: So I tell you what, Crick, should I put my balls on your chin now or later, huh?

jokes.text: Frank: 'Remember the time you crashed my car into the tree? You went crazy and the tire went...' — misremembering/fabricating a nostalgic reunion anecdote
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to participate in reunion nostalgia despite not attending the school
jokes.punchline: He invents (or catastrophically misremembers) a shared memory with Dennis — a car crash — delivered with full confidence
jokes.explanation: Frank's social obliviousness here is funny — he's trying to fake belonging by confabulating memories. The trailing off 'and the tire went...' suggests the memory is either fake or too chaotic to complete. Good Frank character work.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Probably not. Sat behind you in Spanish, remember? Sat... sat right next to you in Algebra one.

jokes.text: Frank sneaks in with a name tag reading 'Nicki Potnick' and immediately starts reminiscing about crashing 'her' car.
jokes.setup: Frank couldn't get in because he's not alumni; he was told to leave.
jokes.punchline: Frank has gotten a name tag for a woman named Nicki Potnick and is now attending the reunion under her identity, complete with a false memory about crashing 'her' car.
jokes.explanation: Frank getting a woman's name tag and immediately starting to construct false memories about her high school experiences is very Frank — chaotic, oblivious, committed to the bit. The 'Nicki Potnick' name is also a funny name in itself.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Wow, I just shook your dead tooth wife. I mean, I had to wash my hands and face.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Nicki Potnick is a girl, okay? And secondly, she's not 65 years old.'
jokes.setup: Frank is wearing Nicki Potnick's name tag.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's objections are both correct and useless — he correctly identifies the two problems with Frank's disguise (wrong gender, wrong age) but neither observation will deter Frank.
jokes.explanation: Good economy — Dennis laying out both defects in Frank's cover story quickly and efficiently. The '65 years old' specification is funny because it acknowledges that Frank looks specifically that old.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't you play coy with me, you little bitch. I'm going to stay right here, and I'm going to wait for my minions to swarm me.

jokes.text: Dennis sits alone at the empty table, and Frank mocks him: 'I thought you were cool. I am cool. Coolest kid here. I'm just posting up, and they're going to come to me.'
jokes.setup: Frank finds Dennis sitting alone at a completely empty table.
jokes.punchline: Dennis insists he's 'posting up' and people will come to him — he's manifested a strategy out of his isolation.
jokes.explanation: The gap between Dennis's declaration ('coolest kid here') and his lonely table is the joke. Frank of all people calling him out on it makes it funnier — if Frank thinks you look uncool, it's terminal.

dialogue.line: Bartender giving Charlie and Mac only 4 drink tickets total, leading to argument about the 'pretty boy' and 'longhair'

jokes.text: Dennis's ex-wife Maureen Ponderosa appears at the reunion to remind him he's late on alimony.
jokes.setup: Dennis says he didn't think about running into his ex-wife because 'I don't think about you.'
jokes.punchline: Maureen has not only found him but has weaponized the reunion as an alimony collection meeting.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the diamond dead tooth joke, but on its own it's fairly standard. Dennis's 'I don't think about you' is a decent character beat — classic Dennis emotional unavailability.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Adriano made fake tickets. Those tickets are fake!

jokes.text: Maureen reveals she has a diamond tooth — which is actually a dead tooth with a diamond in it. 'It wafted over here. The dead tooth... It's burning my nose. It stinks.'
jokes.setup: Maureen says her alimony payments are going to something specific — she reveals a 'diamond tooth.'
jokes.punchline: It's a dead tooth with a diamond on it. Dennis's physical reaction — 'It wafted over here... it's burning my nose' — combined with his line 'Put a diamond on anything that's dead, and it's still dead, Maureen' makes this one of the episode's best moments.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's standout jokes. The concept — a dead tooth with a diamond embedded in it, paid for by alimony — is brilliantly grotesque. Dennis's line 'Put a diamond on anything that's dead, and it's still dead, Maureen' is an almost philosophical observation delivered with genuine disgust. It's well-structured (setup: 'my payments are going somewhere' → reveal: diamond tooth → subversion: it's a rotten dead tooth), original, and fully earned. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Adriano
dialogue.line: Wow. Ronnie the Rat strikes again, huh?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Put a diamond on anything that's dead, and it's still dead, Maureen. It's rotting. Get it out of your face.'
jokes.setup: Maureen has shown Dennis her diamond-embedded dead tooth as a flex
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a philosophical refutation of the diamond tooth concept with the rhythm of genuine wisdom, then ends with 'Get it out of your face'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best single line. 'Put a diamond on anything that's dead, and it's still dead' has the structure of a genuine aphorism, elevated by its application to dental horror. Dennis's contempt is total and his logic is impeccable. The pivot from pseudo-philosophical to 'Get it out of your face' is a perfect landing. Comparable in quotability and economy to the 8.0 anchor. Genuinely exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm going to go to the bathroom, I'm going to find stuff to huff, I'm going to get high. If I'm the Dirtgrub, I'm going to be the Dirtgrub.

jokes.text: Dee announces 'Hello, bitches. That's right. I'm off the wagon. Yeah.' and joins the group.
jokes.setup: Dennis is dealing with Maureen and Frank.
jokes.punchline: Dee's grand entrance — announcing she's 'off the wagon' as if it's a triumph rather than a failure — is a perfect Dee moment of deluded self-presentation.
jokes.explanation: Dee treating her relapse as a power move is very on-brand. 'Hello, bitches' as an entrance is classic Dee delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Charlie, Charlie, don't put the bleach and the ammonia together! It's going to knock the shit out of you.

jokes.text: Dee realizes there's no name tag for her — 'It's like... It's like what? I never existed?'
jokes.setup: Everyone else has been dealing with embarrassing name tags or people who remember them. Dee goes to get hers.
jokes.punchline: There is no name tag for Dee — she was so forgettable in high school that she doesn't even exist in the reunion records. 'It's like I never existed' — which echoes exactly what Mac and Dennis said about her earlier ('most forgettable girl in school').
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback that pays off the earlier 'most forgettable' joke. Dee realizing she literally doesn't exist in the reunion records is devastating and funny in exactly the right way for this show. The beat where she tries to rationalize it ('who cares though, right? 'cause it's high school') before the camera implies a silent moment of genuine pain makes it land harder. High character integration, well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Adriano
dialogue.line: Yeah, probably. That's what these gay guys do, they just... knock each other out with poppers, and then find some kinda rabies-infested rodent to tickle each other's taints with.

jokes.text: Cricket arrives at the reunion — the gang greets him as 'Rickety Cricket' and remarks he looks 'all cleaned up' except for the tooth.
jokes.setup: Someone brings shots to what appears to be the cool table; there's a moment of celebration.
jokes.punchline: It's Cricket — the former priest the gang has progressively destroyed over the series — now cleaned up but still marked by his degradation.
jokes.explanation: Cricket's appearances are always a running gag payoff for longtime viewers. His return to the cloth while still bearing the marks of his degradation is good dark comedy. 'Rickety Cricket, everybody!' is delivered with genuine delight by the gang.

dialogue.speaker: Brad
dialogue.line: I've been waiting a long time for this.

jokes.text: Cricket explains God took him 'into a deep valley, but now I'm soaring on eagle's wings' — Mac responds 'Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. All that, street rat.'
jokes.setup: Cricket is explaining his spiritual redemption arc.
jokes.punchline: Mac dismisses the entire religious testimony with 'Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. All that, street rat.' — refusing to engage with Cricket's attempt at dignity.
jokes.explanation: 'All that, street rat' is an excellent line — it encapsulates the gang's complete disregard for Cricket's humanity in four words. The speed with which Mac dismisses the religious testimony ('Yeah, yeah, yeah') and immediately reverts to 'street rat' is perfectly cruel.

jokes.text: Mac to Cricket: 'Should I put my balls on your chin now or later, huh?'
jokes.setup: Cricket has just finished his speech about God's plan and soaring on eagle's wings.
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to Cricket's spiritual testimony is an immediate, cheerful offer to teabag him — delivered as if it's a scheduling question.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Cricket's earnest religious renewal with Mac's casually crude scheduling question ('now or later?') is very funny. The framing as a simple logistical question — as if teabagging Cricket is on the agenda regardless, just a matter of timing — is a great comedic choice. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: It's her fault. She told me she loved me. We were supposed to be together forever.

jokes.text: Cricket gives everyone at the table a peace blessing, including Frank (Nicki Potnick): 'Peace be to you, my lady.' Frank responds: 'And to you, my son.'
jokes.setup: Cricket is giving peace blessings to everyone.
jokes.punchline: Frank, pretending to be Nicki Potnick (a woman), responds to 'my lady' with 'And to you, my son' — either breaking character or not understanding the exchange.
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'and to you, my son' is funny because it inverts the gender dynamic (he was addressed as a woman but responds as a priest/elder) while also just being a very Frank thing to say. Quick and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, I told him I loved him once, but that was like four years ago.

jokes.text: Mac's response to the entire Cricket peace blessing exchange: 'Boring.'
jokes.setup: Cricket has just done a full peace blessing round.
jokes.punchline: Mac's one-word dismissal of the entire spiritual moment: 'Boring.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word does all the work. Mac's 'Boring' after Cricket's peace blessing is a great character beat: someone who ostensibly cares about God finds Cricket's sincere religiosity tedious. The irony is unacknowledged by Mac, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.line: Cricket's revelation about stealing jewelry and being covered in ringworm after Dee told him she loved him

jokes.text: An unknown woman appears and tries to get people to remember her ('Sat behind you in Spanish,' 'Sat right next to you in Algebra 1') — nobody knows who she is.
jokes.setup: Someone appears at the reunion excited to reconnect.
jokes.punchline: Absolutely nobody recognizes her — 'Who the hell is that? I don't know. I've never seen her before in my life.' She's the ultimate 'most forgettable person in school.'
jokes.explanation: A great structural callback to the 'most forgettable girl in school' line — the show immediately demonstrates what that looks like in practice. The cruel comedy of someone desperately reciting their seating arrangements ('Algebra 1!') while nobody has any memory of them is excellent cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Adriano
dialogue.line: To think I was going to let you jack me off...

jokes.text: Dee immediately recognizes the unknown woman and says 'I know you, bitch. I know you, bitch.' — but only to protect her own social standing at the cool table.
jokes.setup: Everyone is denying knowing the unknown woman.
jokes.punchline: Dee does recognize her — 'I know you, bitch' — but the cruelty of the delivery and the context (Dee protecting her status at the cool table) reveals she's denying any real connection.
jokes.explanation: Dee recognizing the woman but calling her 'bitch' (twice) while apparently protecting her new cool-table status is a great Dee moment — she's doing to this woman exactly what was done to her. The repetition of 'I know you, bitch' is weirdly rhythmic and funny.

jokes.text: Dee declares herself 'queen of the night' at the cool table — the visual of her surrounded by people who mocked her for years.
jokes.setup: Dee has successfully infiltrated the cool table.
jokes.punchline: Dee proclaims herself 'queen of the night' — a massively deluded self-assessment given she's sitting with people who gave her the nickname 'Aluminum Monster.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee delusional triumph. The irony is rich — she's celebrating being accepted by the people who psychologically damaged her — but it's a fairly predictable Dee beat.

jokes.text: Frank reacts to Maureen's dead diamond tooth: 'Wow! I just shook your dead-tooth wife. I mean, I had to wash my hands and face.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just met Maureen.
jokes.punchline: Frank's visceral reaction — having to wash hands AND face after meeting her — amplifies the horror of the dead tooth. The 'and face' detail is what makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: The 'and face' addition is the specific detail that elevates this from a standard 'that person is gross' joke to something funnier. Frank of all people being grossed out by someone says a lot.

jokes.text: Tim Murphy appears — the man who slept with Dennis's prom date — and Dennis's immediate shift from charming to seething is visible in his reaction.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis are discussing Maureen; Dennis notices someone.
jokes.punchline: Tim Murphy — introduced as 'the asshole that slept with my prom date' — is at the reunion. Frank's 'Va va voom' on seeing Tim's wife makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the Dennis/Tim dynamic that runs through the episode. Frank's 'va va voom' on seeing Tim's wife is a quick funny beat. Mostly setup.

jokes.text: Dennis to Tim Murphy: 'I won't be going anywhere with you, Tim... Don't you play coy with me, you little bitch.'
jokes.setup: Tim, seeming perfectly friendly, invites Dennis to come join his table.
jokes.punchline: Dennis responds as if Tim is playing some kind of psychological game — 'don't play coy with me, you little bitch' — when Tim appears to be genuinely just being friendly, making Dennis look unhinged.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's paranoid intensity toward someone who is behaving completely normally is a great character beat. 'Don't play coy with me, you little bitch' directed at someone who just said 'why don't you come join our table?' is perfectly unhinged Dennis energy. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I'm going to stay right here, and I'm going to wait for my minions to swarm me. And swarm they will, Tim.'
jokes.setup: Tim has invited Dennis to join his table.
jokes.punchline: Dennis insists he's waiting for 'minions' to swarm him — the vocabulary of supervillainy applied to a high school reunion. The camera presumably shows an empty table.
jokes.explanation: 'Minions' and 'swarm' are perfect word choices for Dennis — the vocabulary of a narcissistic supervillain who is currently sitting alone at an empty table. 'And swarm they will, Tim' as a dramatic declaration is very quotable. High character integration.

jokes.text: Tim says 'Same old Dennis Reynolds' as a parting observation — then accidentally calls Frank 'Nicki,' saying 'You look good, Nicki.' Frank: 'Thank you, Tim!'
jokes.setup: Tim is leaving after the Dennis interaction.
jokes.punchline: Tim sees Frank and compliments 'Nicki Potnick' — validating Frank's terrible disguise. Frank's delighted 'Thank you, Tim!' suggests he's fully committing to being Nicki Potnick.
jokes.explanation: The fact that Tim actually accepts Frank as Nicki Potnick — despite Frank being a 65-year-old man — is a great beat. It implies either Tim has terrible memory, doesn't know Nicki, or is too polite to say anything. Frank's enthusiastic acceptance of the compliment is very funny.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie trying to get drinks: 'Six beers for the two of us, please.' — immediately corrected to 'Drink tickets for the two of us, please.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie need drinks to 'get their mojo back.'
jokes.punchline: Mac's first instinct is to order six beers for two people before realizing there's a ticket system — the casual assumption of overconsumption is funny.
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — the 'six beers for two people' as a baseline expectation is a decent character note. Sets up the ticket argument.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie argue about the math of two drink tickets per person: 'That's only two per person, bozo.' / 'Well, how am I supposed to get drunk off of only four beers?'
jokes.setup: They've received four drink tickets total.
jokes.punchline: Mac complains that four beers isn't enough to get drunk — Charlie correctly points out that's two per person. Mac's question ('how am I supposed to get drunk off of only four beers?') reveals they expected to drink far more than a sane amount.
jokes.explanation: Their mutual 'bozo' insults and the casual assumption that four beers is insufficient quantity reveals their baseline dysfunction. Functional comic beat.

jokes.text: Mac tells the bartender 'I didn't ask you, pretty boy. It's a conversation between me and the longhair.'
jokes.setup: The bartender tries to explain the two-ticket-per-person rule.
jokes.punchline: Mac distinguishes between 'pretty boy' (the well-dressed bartender he dislikes) and 'the longhair' (a different bartender he prefers to negotiate with). The specificity of the nicknames is very Mac.
jokes.explanation: 'The longhair' is a great Mac-specific detail — he's categorizing people by physical type as if they're different species to negotiate with. The dismissal of 'pretty boy' is classic Mac insecurity/aggression.

jokes.text: Mac's response to being called a fat bitch: 'You're making this about weight?' / Charlie: 'He's gained a lot of weight.' / Mac: 'I'm not going to take some shit from some bartender.' / Charlie: 'You're a bartender. He doesn't know that!'
jokes.setup: Mac is furious at being called a fat bitch by the bartender.
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes professional dignity as a bartender to dismiss the other bartender's opinion — Charlie correctly notes the bartender doesn't know Mac is also a bartender, making the status claim meaningless.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's 'You're a bartender. He doesn't know that!' is an excellent beat — it perfectly dissects why Mac's professional dignity claim is completely useless while also inadvertently being correct. The logic is broken but internally consistent in a very Sunny way.

jokes.text: Adriano reveals he printed 'like a hundred' fake drink tickets at the computer lab: 'Way more than I need.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are struggling with their two-ticket limit.
jokes.punchline: Adriano waltzes in with an enormous stack of fake tickets printed at the computer lab — the gap between Mac and Charlie's pathetic situation and Adriano's casual abundance is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Way more than I need' is good — the casual abundance and the 'computer lab' detail (a school reunion still has a computer lab available, and Adriano used it to print fake tickets) is funny. Sets up the rat callback.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie beg Adriano for some fake tickets — he refuses them but immediately gives some to another person who is 'cool.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie desperately ask for some of Adriano's fake tickets.
jokes.punchline: Adriano refuses them, then immediately hands tickets to someone else because they're 'cool' — the gap between Mac and Charlie's desperation and their social status is crystallized.
jokes.explanation: The cringe of watching Mac and Charlie get explicitly ranked below a random 'cool' person is good. 'Well, that guy's cool, so...' as the entire explanation is funny in its casual cruelty.

jokes.text: Mac rats out Adriano's fake tickets to the bartender: 'Adriano made fake tickets! Those tickets are fake! He gets to drink and we don't. That's not fair!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have an 'excellent plan' to get drinks.
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'excellent plan' is to immediately rat out Adriano to the bartender — an act of pure informing driven entirely by spite. This is 'Ronnie the Rat' behavior in real time.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best structural jokes because it's a perfect character callback — Mac's first instinct under social pressure is to rat someone out, exactly as he did in high school. His 'That's not fair!' adds a childish quality that makes it funnier. The structure is excellent: Mac sets up an 'excellent plan' → the plan is immediately revealed as snitching → everyone immediately calls him Ronnie the Rat. It's the episode's themes made concrete.

jokes.text: After Mac rats out Adriano, Charlie mocks him: 'Ha, ha! You got in trouble. You got in trouble!' — and then everyone calls Mac 'Ronnie the Rat strikes again.'
jokes.setup: Mac's snitching has gotten Adriano's tickets confiscated.
jokes.punchline: 'Ronnie the Rat strikes again, huh?' — the high school nickname is immediately reactivated, confirming that Mac hasn't changed at all in 15 years. Charlie's childish 'You got in trouble!' is funny as a separate beat.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the rat joke. 'Ronnie the Rat strikes again' as a verdict on Mac's character is very satisfying structurally. Charlie's 'You got in trouble! You got in trouble!' is an additional funny beat — Charlie gleefully mocking Mac in a very childish way, then immediately blaming Mac for getting them all in trouble.

jokes.text: Charlie declares 'If I'm the Dirtgrub, I'm going to be the Dirtgrub' and decides to find stuff to huff and 'get sad.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to tell Charlie things don't have to go this way.
jokes.punchline: Charlie fully embraces his high school identity — 'I'll get high. I'll get sad. People can laugh at me.' — delivered with heartbreaking resignation wrapped in comedic commitment.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most purely Charlie moments. 'I'll get high. I'll get sad. People can laugh at me. I hate high school, man!' is both funny and genuinely sad. The character specificity is off the charts — only Charlie Kelly has this exact relationship with his own degradation. 'I hate high school, man!' as a punctuation is perfect.

jokes.text: Frank tries to get people to rehearse Plan B — Dee's old back brace — immediately outside the reunion
jokes.setup: Charlie has stormed off to huff inhalants; Mac is upset
jokes.punchline: Frank has retrieved Dee's old back brace from the car and wants to rehearse 'Plan B' — which is apparently using the brace for some scheme
jokes.explanation: The Plan B payoff (it involves Dee's back brace) is funnier for being so stupid. Frank's enthusiasm and the timing — suggesting rehearsal while everything is falling apart around them — is good Frank character work. The full Plan B execution is presumably saved for Part 2.

jokes.text: Charlie combines bleach and ammonia to make inhalants; Mac warns him 'it's going to knock the shit out of you'; Charlie insists 'Don't tell me how to mix my own inhalants. I know how to do inhalants.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has found chemicals to huff in what appears to be a school bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Charlie asserting expertise in inhalant-mixing ('I know how to do my own inhalants, okay?') while making a potentially lethal combination is both very dark and very funny. The professional pride in his drug use is the joke.
jokes.explanation: "Don't tell me how to mix my own inhalants" is an instantly quotable line. Charlie taking professional pride in his inhalant knowledge — there's a right and wrong way to do this, and he knows — is deeply character-specific and very dark. The 'I know how to do inhalants' assertion of expertise is excellent. High quotability, very high character integration.

jokes.text: Charlie knocks himself out with the bleach/ammonia combination — Mac and Frank look at him and simply say 'Whoops-a-daisy. That's it. Well, let's just wait till he wakes up.'
jokes.setup: Mac has warned Charlie the combination will knock him out.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately knocks himself out. Mac and Frank's response is a breezy 'Whoops-a-daisy. That's it. Well, let's just wait till he wakes up' — completely unphased by their friend being unconscious from a toxic gas mixture.
jokes.explanation: 'Whoops-a-daisy. That's it. Well, let's just wait till he wakes up' is perfect deadpan. The gang's total lack of concern for Charlie's chemical unconsciousness is excellent character work. The 'Whoops-a-daisy' specifically — such a mild verbal response to someone being knocked out by toxic fumes — is a great word choice.

jokes.text: Adriano and crew discover Charlie unconscious in the bathroom and Mac is exposed as 'Nicki Potnick.' Adriano: 'Looks like you had a rough couple of years there, Nicki.'
jokes.setup: Adriano's crew finds the trio in the bathroom with Charlie unconscious on the floor.
jokes.punchline: Frank is immediately clocked as 'Nicki Potnick' by Adriano who apparently went to school with her — but Frank responds as a man: 'Uh, yeah. I'm a guy now.'
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Adriano apparently knew Nicki Potnick well enough to comment on her 'rough couple of years' — while Frank maintains the ruse by saying 'I'm a guy now' — is well-constructed. Frank's straight-faced 'I'm a guy now' as his entire explanation for his appearance is excellent.

jokes.text: Mac describes what 'these gay guys do' to explain Charlie's unconscious state: 'They knock each other out with poppers and then find some kinda rabies-infested rodent to tickle each other's taints with.'
jokes.setup: Adriano asks what they're doing 'perving out on Dirtgrub.'
jokes.punchline: Mac's alternative explanation for Charlie's unconsciousness — attributing it to a bizarre gay sex ritual involving poppers and rabies-infested rodents — is so specifically absurd that it functions as a Rorschach test for Mac's anxieties.
jokes.explanation: The 'rabies-infested rodent to tickle each other's taints' is the kind of specific absurdist escalation that only Sunny does. Mac inventing this entire ritual — and then denying involvement in it while also being somehow familiar with it — is great character work. The specificity ('rabies-infested') is what makes it funny rather than just crude.

jokes.text: Mac invokes being a 'respected businessman' to Adriano's crew — while standing over an unconscious Charlie in a school bathroom.
jokes.setup: Adriano's crew is about to give Mac and Frank a wedgie/beat them up.
jokes.punchline: Mac's appeal is to his status as a 'grown adult' and 'respected businessman' — said while in a bathroom next to an unconscious man who huffed cleaning products.
jokes.explanation: The gap between Mac's self-presentation ('respected businessman') and reality (bathroom, unconscious Charlie, about to be bullied) is the joke. Classic Sunny irony.

jokes.text: Adriano's crew physically attacks Mac and Frank in the bathroom — 'Ow! My balls! Aaah!' — while Charlie remains unconscious on the floor.
jokes.setup: Mac's 'respected businessman' appeal has failed.
jokes.punchline: They get beaten up — specifically 'my balls' — while Charlie sleeps through the entire thing on the floor.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy lands mostly because of the setup and the detail of Charlie remaining unconscious throughout. 'My balls' as a battle cry is functional but not especially crafted. The image is funny.

jokes.text: Mac and Frank emerge from the bathroom beaten up, and Dee is dancing near them: 'You guys just missed something so awesome that we did. Heed my warning.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank come out of the bathroom having just been beaten up.
jokes.punchline: Dee, completely unaware, claims she did something awesome and warns them about Adriano's group — not realizing they just got beaten up by that same group.
jokes.explanation: The irony of Dee warning them about the group that just assaulted them is a decent beat, but it's fairly light. 'Heed my warning' is a funny Dee-ism.

jokes.text: Dennis approaches Tim Murphy's group: 'Can you believe I came to this thing? I was posted up over there. You guys probably didn't see me.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been sitting alone for most of the episode; he finally approaches Tim's table.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's opener is to ask if they saw him 'posted up' — fishing for validation while pretending to be casual. 'No reason to be intimidated. You know? I'm a human being, after all.'
jokes.explanation: 'No reason to be intimidated. You know? I'm a human being, after all' — Dennis reassuring people not to be intimidated by him, to a table of people who are not intimidated by him, is perfect Dennis Reynolds energy. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Multiple people at Tim's table discover wallets, necklaces, and gold chains are missing — 'Oh, my God, my necklace is missing. / Oh, come on! My gold chain's gone.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just joined Tim's table.
jokes.punchline: Everyone at the table discovers their valuables are missing simultaneously — implying Frank has been pickpocketing the reunion.
jokes.explanation: The escalating discovery of multiple stolen items is well-paced and reveals Frank has been operating as a career criminal throughout the reunion. The 'with all the security' commentary is funny given the security let an old man in with a woman's name tag.

jokes.text: Cricket is spotted wearing multiple stolen chains around his neck — 'Wait a second, Mara. What is that around your neck?' / 'Oh, that's, uh, probably just a scar that...'
jokes.setup: Everyone is looking for their stolen valuables.
jokes.punchline: Cricket is wearing all the stolen jewelry — but his initial attempt to pass the chains off as 'scars' is the joke. The misdirection (we expect Frank to be the thief, it's Cricket with the goods) adds a twist.
jokes.explanation: Cricket's 'that's probably just a scar' as his initial explanation for a pile of jewelry is very funny — it shows just how practiced he is at covering up his criminal behavior. The reveal that it's Cricket, not Frank, with the stolen goods is a good misdirect.

jokes.text: Cricket's breakdown: 'I've sinned! My God, you are covered in ringworm.' / 'It's her fault. She told me she loved me. We were supposed to be together forever.'
jokes.setup: Cricket has been caught with the stolen jewelry.
jokes.punchline: Cricket immediately has a full breakdown — confessing to sins, revealing ringworm (from Dee), and that Dee told him she loved him and they were supposed to be 'together forever.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'caught with jewelry' to 'ringworm confession' to 'we were supposed to be together forever' is a perfect Sunny sequence — each revelation is worse. Cricket's desperate romantic declaration about Dee in front of a crowd is both deeply funny and sad. 'She told me she loved me' as his criminal defense is excellent.

jokes.text: Dee's response to being accused of a romantic relationship with Cricket: 'No! Me, with him? I... What, are you crazy? No!' — then: 'Yeah, I told him I loved him once, but that was four years ago.'
jokes.setup: Cricket has claimed Dee told him she loved him.
jokes.punchline: Dee's categorical denial collapses immediately — she did say it, four years ago, as a one-off. The 'but that was four years ago' as if it makes it okay is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: The speed of the denial-to-admission is very Sunny. Dee's 'but that was four years ago' as if that's a sufficient defense for leading someone on enough that they're carrying jewelry on their person and declaring eternal love is a perfect Dee beat. The structure of full denial → grudging partial admission is clean.

jokes.text: Cricket: 'To think I was going to let you jack me off.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just admitted she told Cricket she loved him.
jokes.punchline: Cricket's additional revelation — that he was going to allow Dee to perform a sexual act — is delivered with wounded dignity as if it's a sacrifice he was going to make.
jokes.explanation: The framing — 'I was going to LET you' — is what makes this exceptional. Cricket frames the sexual act as a generous concession on his part, as if Dee should be grateful. The wounded dignity of a man who is objectively the least desirable person at the reunion claiming to be doing Dee a favor is perfectly inverted and very dark. High quotability, great economy.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Wait, wait. You were?' — a beat where Dee actually seems to consider that she missed out on something.
jokes.setup: Cricket has revealed he was going to 'let' Dee perform a sexual act.
jokes.punchline: Dee's 'Wait, wait. You were?' — a pause where she seems genuinely interested rather than horrified — is the punchline. The implication that Dee's options are so limited that Cricket's offer was appealing.
jokes.explanation: Four words — 'Wait, wait. You were?' — do an enormous amount of work. It implies Dee's self-image is so low that Cricket's offer was a genuine prospect. The beat relies entirely on the audience understanding how pathetic both parties are, which is perfect character-integrated comedy. Very high economy.

jokes.text: The group drags Cricket out of the reunion while he screams 'No, no, no! Come on. We're cool! Yeah, we're like the...' — then gets physically removed.
jokes.setup: Cricket's breakdown and theft are exposed.
jokes.punchline: 'We're cool! Yeah, we're like the...' — Cricket can't even complete his claim to social status before being dragged out. The unfinished sentence is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The unfinished 'We're like the...' is a great comedic choice — Cricket is trying to invoke some social identity and can't even complete the claim before being removed. Good structural choice.

tmdb_overview: The gang have much to prove when they attend their high-school reunion. They meet old friends and make new foes as they stroll down memory lane.
